name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
title: Motion Capture and Retargeting
answer: Motion capture and retargeting covers the recording of human or object movement and the transfer of that movement onto a digital skeleton or character. It is used in film and game animation, dance documentation, live performance, biomechanics, and virtual production. Retargeting is the specific step of mapping motion from one body or rig to another, often with different proportions or joint structures. In choreography and motion mapping, the focus is on preserving the expressive qualities of a dancer's movement while making it usable on a digital avatar or a different performer.

sections.body: Motion capture and retargeting covers the recording of human or object movement and the transfer of that movement onto a digital skeleton or character. It is used in film and game animation, dance documentation, live performance, biomechanics, and virtual production. Retargeting is the specific step of mapping motion from one body or rig to another, often with different proportions or joint structures. In choreography and motion mapping, the focus is on preserving the expressive qualities of a dancer's movement while making it usable on a digital avatar or a different performer.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of capture hardware and animation software. Optical systems such as Vicon and OptiTrack use multiple cameras and reflective markers, while inertial suits from Xsens and Rokoko use accelerometers and gyroscopes. Markerless approaches use ordinary video cameras and pose estimation models. On the software side, MotionBuilder, Blender, Unreal Engine, Unity, and Maya are common for solving, cleaning, and retargeting motion. Data is typically stored in formats like BVH, FBX, or C3D.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline starts with calibration and a capture session, where a performer wears markers or a suit and acts out the movement. The system then solves the data into joint positions or rotations, which are cleaned to remove noise and gaps. Retargeting maps that solved motion onto a target rig, adjusting for limb length, joint limits, and foot contact. Animators then refine the result, adding corrections and secondary motion, or use AI models to automate parts of the retargeting and style transfer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around motion capture center on consent, ownership, and provenance. A performer's motion can be personal data, and contracts or union agreements often govern how it may be reused. Choreography may be protected by copyright, and retargeting a recorded performance onto a new character can raise questions about derivative works. Provenance matters because it is hard to tell where a motion clip came from once it is retargeted, so studios increasingly track source, consent, and license terms. There is also risk of bias in pose estimation for different body types, clothing, or skin tones.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time markerless capture and AI-driven retargeting that can preserve an individual's movement style. Generative motion models are beginning to create new motion from text prompts or short examples, which could change how choreography is authored and reused. Virtual production and live performance are likely to adopt these tools as they become more reliable. The main open questions are ethical and economic: how performers are credited and compensated when their motion is retargeted, and how provenance is maintained across automated pipelines.
